# Overview

Exercise 4 built a spatial weights matrix and used it to compute a spatially lagged GDP per capita
(GDPPC) for each of Hunan's 88 counties. At the end of that exercise, the scatterplot of GDPPC
against its spatial lag had a positive slope. This suggested that counties with high GDPPC are
adjacent to other counties with high GDPPC. No test was made of whether that slope is larger than
spatial randomness would produce.

This exercise tests for spatial autocorrelation in two ways. A **global** measure is a single
statistic for the whole province, tested against the null hypothesis of spatial randomness. A
**local** measure is computed for each county, and identifies the counties that belong to a cluster
and the counties that differ from their neighbours.

**Part 1** reproduces r4gdsa chapter 9, Global Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation: Moran's I,
Geary's C, their Monte Carlo versions and the spatial correlogram. **Part 2** reproduces chapter 10,
Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation: local Moran's I with the LISA cluster map, and the
Getis-Ord Gi\* hot spot map. **Part 3** examines the method of the two chapters and adds the parts
of the lecture that neither chapter covers.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}

## Sources

The hands-on exercise is two chapters, both assigned for Lesson 5:

- [Chapter 9: Global Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation](https://r4gdsa.netlify.app/chap09.html)
- [Chapter 10: Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation](https://r4gdsa.netlify.app/chap10.html)

The Lesson 5 outline sets five papers as self-reading. Each is used in a specific section.

| Reading | What it contributes | Used in |
|---|---|---|
| **Moran (1950)**, "Notes on Continuous Stochastic Phenomena" | The statistic, derived for a regular lattice; the expectation −1/(N−1); and the statement that the variance needs a normality assumption while the expectation does not | 3.3, 5.5 |
| **Geary (1954)**, "The Contiguity Ratio and Statistical Mapping" | The squared-difference form, and the clearest statement of what each of the two null models assumes | 3.4, 5.5, 5.6 |
| **Getis and Ord (1992)**, "The Analysis of Spatial Association by Use of Distance Statistics" | The G statistic in both forms, the binary symmetric weights it is defined on, the requirement of a natural origin, and the demonstration that Moran's I cannot tell high-value clustering from low-value clustering | 4.2, 5.4 |
| **Anselin (1995)**, "Local Indicators of Spatial Association - LISA" | The two conditions a statistic must satisfy to be a LISA; a Bonferroni-corrected worked example run on 9,999 permutations; and the claim that permutation inference is identical for the local Moran and both of Gi and Gi\* | 4.1, 5.3, 5.8 |
| **Ord and Getis (1995)**, "Local Spatial Autocorrelation Statistics: Distributional Issues and an Application" | Simulation evidence for when a normal approximation to a local statistic fails, the extension of Gi to nonbinary weights, and the Bonferroni recommendation | 5.2, 5.3 |

The outline also lists eight references. Three of them are used on this page:

| Reference | What it contributes | Used in |
|---|---|---|
| **Anselin (1996)**, "The Moran Scatterplot as an ESDA Tool" | Moran's I as the slope of the regression of the spatial lag on the variable, and the four-quadrant reading of the scatterplot | 4.1.4 |
| **Getis (2010)**, "Spatial Autocorrelation", chapter B.3 of the *Handbook of Applied Spatial Analysis* | The problem of dependent multiple tests in local statistics, and the false discovery rate as one response to it | 5.3.1 |
| **Mack and Kam (2018)**, "Is There Space for Violence?" | A tabulation of neighbour counts across weights definitions before one is chosen | 5.7.1 |

The other five references on the outline are not used on this page.

:::

## Differences from the chapters

| | The chapter | This page | Why | Where |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Projected CRS** | chapter 10 uses EPSG:32650, chapter 9 does not project at all | EPSG:32649 throughout | Hunan spans 108.78°E to 114.25°E, so it lies in UTM zone 49N. Zone 50N starts at 114°E. The wrong zone narrows the fixed bandwidth from 62,955 m to 60,800 m, a 3.4% change on the correct figure | 5.1 |
| **Local p-values** | `nsim = 99` is passed, then `p_ii` is used | `p_ii_sim`, with `nsim = 999` | Both come from the same permutations, but `p_ii` is a normal approximation to a distribution the same call reports as skewed. The choice changes the count of significant counties from 13 to 16 and changes which ones | 5.2 |
| **Number of simulations** | chapter 10 uses 99 for the local statistics | 999 | A rank-based p-value cannot fall below `2 / (nsim + 1)`, so at 99 its minimum is 0.02, above the Bonferroni bound for 88 counties. Chapter 9 already uses 999 | 5.2, 5.3 |
| **Multiple comparisons** | not mentioned | measured, with the positions of both assigned papers | Ord and Getis (1995) recommend Bonferroni and Anselin (1995) applies it. 88 tests at α = 0.05 expect about four false positives, and at `nsim = 999` no county remains significant under either correction | 5.3 |
| **Natural origin of the G variable** | standardises `GDPPC` for the scatterplot and uses the raw values for Gi\*, without saying why | tested by shifting GDPPC | Getis and Ord (1992) state that G is scale-invariant but not location-invariant. Adding 100,000 to GDPPC changes the p-value of global G from 0.0012 to 0.19 and leaves Moran's I unchanged | 5.4.1 |
| **Gi against the local Moran** | presented as separate analyses | the permutation inference compared directly | Anselin (1995) claims it is identical for the local Moran, Gi and Gi\*. On these weights it holds for all three, up to simulation error, so chapter 10's two maps differ in their weights and in how they label counties | 5.8 |
| **Standardised Moran scatterplot** | `scale(lag_GDPPC)` on the vertical axis | the lag of the standardised variable, as in Anselin (1996) | Standardising the lag separately makes the slope of the fitted line 0.485, the Pearson correlation of GDPPC with its lag, where Moran's I is 0.301 | 4.1.4 |
| **Choice of `k` for Gi\*** | `k = 6`, not examined | `k` = 4, 6 and 8 compared | Significant counties rise from 17 to 25 with `k`; twelve keep the same classification under every value | 5.7.1 |
| **Getis-Ord global G** | not covered | added, with `globalG.test()` | Slides 16 and 17 cover it and neither chapter reaches it | 5.4 |
| **Local Geary's c** | not covered | added, with `local_c_perm()` | Slide 26 names it as the other LISA. It finds 21 significant counties where local Moran's I finds 16 | 5.6 |
| **Adaptive distance weights** | computed as `hunan_adw`, never used | used, and compared against the fixed band | The chapter builds the object and then runs Gi\* on the fixed-band weights only. The two disagree on 15 of the 88 counties | 5.7 |
| **Moran's I null model** | `randomisation = TRUE` default, not discussed | the three null models explained from the assigned readings | The default z-score and the permutation test in Part 1 rest on different assumptions, and Moran's own variance assumes normality | 5.5 |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

# Getting started

## Packages

`spdep` provides the global statistics and the correlogram. `sfdep` provides the local statistics,
returning them as columns of a data frame. The two give identical local Moran values. `sfdep` avoids
the matrix that `spdep` returns, which has to be bound to the sf object by row position.

```{r}
pacman::p_load(sf, spdep, sfdep, tmap, tidyverse, knitr)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses one function:

```r
pacman::p_load(..., install = TRUE)                       # pacman
```

- `p_load()` loads each package named in `...`, and first installs any that are missing, because
  `install = TRUE` is the default. It replaces a separate `install.packages()` and `library()` call
  for each package.
- The `pacman::` prefix calls the function from `pacman` without attaching the package itself.
:::

## The data

Both chapters use the same two files as Chapter 8, described in Exercise 4.

| Layer | Format | Features | Native CRS | Contents |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Hunan` | ESRI shapefile | 88 polygons | WGS 84, EPSG:4326 | County boundaries of Hunan province |
| `Hunan_2012` | CSV | 88 rows, 29 fields | not spatial | 2012 development indicators by county |

### County boundaries

The shapefile is in geographic coordinates (degrees). Contiguity is defined by shared boundaries and
is unaffected by the projection, but every distance-based weight depends on the projection. Section
5.1 identifies the UTM zone for Hunan as zone 49N (EPSG:32649), and the layer is projected to that
zone here so that one CRS is used throughout the page.

```{r}
hunan <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", layer = "Hunan", quiet = TRUE) |>
  st_transform(crs = 32649)
st_crs(hunan)$input
nrow(hunan)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses three functions and the pipe:

```r
st_read(dsn, layer, quiet = FALSE)                        # sf
st_transform(x, crs)                                      # sf
st_crs(x)                                                 # sf
```

- `st_read()` reads a vector data file into an sf data frame: one row per feature, with attribute
  columns and a geometry column. For a shapefile, `dsn` is the folder and `layer` is the file name
  without its extension. `quiet = TRUE` suppresses the summary it otherwise prints, which begins
  with the full path of the data folder on the computer that renders the page.
- `|>` is R's native pipe. It passes the result on its left as the first argument of the function on
  its right, so `st_transform()` receives the layer from `st_read()` as its `x`.
- `st_transform()` recalculates every coordinate in the CRS given in `crs`, here EPSG:32649, UTM
  zone 49N, in metres. `st_set_crs()` would change only the label, and leave the coordinates in
  degrees.
- `st_crs()` returns the CRS of an object, and `$input` extracts the code it was set from. `nrow()`
  counts the counties.

The figure shows what `st_transform()` does to the layer.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4
ortho <- "+proj=ortho +lat_0=27.5 +lon_0=111.5 +datum=WGS84"
s2_was <- sf_use_s2(FALSE)
globe_land <- spData::world |> st_crop(xmin = 50, xmax = 170, ymin = -30, ymax = 80)
globe_grid <- st_graticule(st_bbox(c(xmin = 50, ymin = -30, xmax = 170, ymax = 80), crs = 4326),
                           lon = seq(60, 170, 20), lat = seq(-20, 80, 20))
sf_use_s2(s2_was)
globe_disc <- st_sfc(st_buffer(st_point(c(0, 0)), 6371000), crs = ortho)
hunan_deg <- st_transform(hunan, 4326)

before <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = globe_disc, fill = "aliceblue", colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_sf(data = globe_grid, colour = "grey75", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = globe_land, fill = "grey88", colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = hunan_deg, fill = "darkorange", colour = NA) +
  coord_sf(crs = ortho) +
  labs(title = "Before: degrees on the globe", subtitle = "EPSG:4326, latitude and longitude") +
  theme_void()

step <- ggplot() +
  annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = 1, y = 0, yend = 0,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm")), linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.12, label = "st_transform(crs = 32649)",
           family = "mono", size = 2.8) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.1, 1.1), ylim = c(-0.5, 0.5), clip = "off") +
  theme_void()

after <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = hunan, fill = "darkorange", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  coord_sf(datum = 32649) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "After: metres on a flat grid", subtitle = "EPSG:32649, UTM zone 49N",
       x = "easting (m)", y = "northing (m)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 7))

patchwork::wrap_plots(before, step, after, widths = c(1, 0.7, 1))
```
:::

### Development indicators

```{r}
hunan2012 <- read_csv("data/aspatial/Hunan_2012.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
dim(hunan2012)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses one function:

```r
read_csv(file, show_col_types = should_show_types())      # readr
```

- `read_csv()` reads a comma-separated file into a tibble and guesses the type of each column from
  its values. `show_col_types = FALSE` suppresses the message that lists those guesses.
- `dim()` returns the number of rows and columns.

The two files are read by different functions, which return different kinds of object:

| | `read_csv()` | `st_read()` |
|---|---|---|
| Package | `readr`, part of the tidyverse | `sf` |
| Reads | a table of values, here a CSV file | a spatial file, here a shapefile |
| Returns | a tibble (`tbl_df`), a kind of data frame | an sf data frame: a data frame with a geometry column |
| Geometry and CRS | none | one polygon per row, with its CRS |
| On this page | `Hunan_2012`: 88 rows, 29 columns of indicators | `Hunan`: 88 county polygons with 7 attribute fields |
| Role on this page | supplies GDPPC, the variable every statistic tests | supplies the county boundaries, from which the maps are drawn and the neighbours found |

`left_join()` in the next section attaches the CSV's columns to the county polygons, so that GDPPC
and the geometry are in one sf object.
:::

## Joining the two

```{r}
hunan <- left_join(hunan, hunan2012, by = "County") |>
  select(1:4, 7, 15)
names(hunan)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses two functions:

```r
left_join(x, y, by = NULL)                                # dplyr
select(.data, ...)                                        # dplyr
```

- `left_join()` keeps every row of `x`, here `hunan` with its geometry, and adds the columns of `y`
  from the matching row. `by` names the column to match on. With the default, `NULL`, it matches on
  every column name the two tables share and prints a message naming them. Chapter 9 relies on that
  default. This chunk names `by = "County"`, as in Exercise 4, which fixes the match to one column.
- `select()` keeps the columns listed in `...`, given as names or as positions. `1:4, 7, 15` are
  positions in the joined table. On an sf object the geometry column is kept without being listed.

The joined table has 36 columns. Columns 8 to 35 come from the CSV. The columns that `select()`
keeps are shaded:

<table class="table table-sm">
<tr><th style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">1</th><th style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">2</th><th style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">3</th><th style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">4</th><th>5</th><th>6</th><th style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">7</th><th>8</th><th>…</th><th style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">15</th><th>…</th><th style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">36</th></tr>
<tr><td style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">NAME_2</td><td style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">ID_3</td><td style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">NAME_3</td><td style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">ENGTYPE_3</td><td>Shape_Leng</td><td>Shape_Area</td><td style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">County</td><td>City</td><td>…</td><td style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">GDPPC</td><td>…</td><td style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">geometry</td></tr>
</table>

Selection by position depends on this column order. The printed names confirm that the six
attributes kept are the ones intended.

The same columns can be selected by name, which does not depend on the column order and states what
is kept:

```r
hunan <- left_join(hunan, hunan2012, by = "County") |>
  select(NAME_2, ID_3, NAME_3, ENGTYPE_3, County, GDPPC)
```

Both versions return the same object. The page keeps the chapter's positions so that its code
matches chapter 9.
:::

# Part 1: Global measures of spatial autocorrelation

This part follows r4gdsa [Chapter 9](https://r4gdsa.netlify.app/chap09.html). Each statistic in it
is a single value for the whole province, tested against the null hypothesis of spatial randomness.

## Mapping GDPPC

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.1
equal <- tm_shape(hunan) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "GDPPC",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "equal", n = 5,
                                              values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "GDPPC",
                                      position = tm_pos_out("right", "center"))) +
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Equal interval classification")

quantile <- tm_shape(hunan) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "GDPPC",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5,
                                              values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "GDPPC",
                                      position = tm_pos_out("right", "center"))) +
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Quantile classification")

tmap_arrange(equal, quantile, asp = 1, ncol = 2)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses eight functions:

```r
tm_shape(shp)                                             # tmap
tm_polygons(fill, fill.scale, fill.legend)                # tmap
tm_scale_intervals(n = 5, style = "pretty", values = NA)  # tmap
tm_legend(title, position)                                # tmap
tm_pos_out(cell.h, cell.v)                                # tmap
tm_borders(col, col_alpha)                                # tmap
tm_title(text)                                            # tmap
tmap_arrange(..., ncol = NA, asp = 0)                     # tmap
```

- `tm_shape()` names the sf object that the layers after it draw. Each `+` adds a layer or a
  setting.
- `tm_polygons()` draws the polygons. Each visual property in tmap v4 has three arguments: `fill`
  names the variable that sets the colour, `fill.scale` sets how its values map to colours, and
  `fill.legend` sets the legend.
- `tm_scale_intervals()` divides a numeric variable into `n` classes by the method in `style`, and
  colours them from the palette in `values`, here the ColorBrewer Blues palette. The default style
  is `"pretty"`. Only `style` differs between the two maps.
- `tm_legend()` sets the legend title and position. `tm_pos_out("right", "center")` places the
  legend outside the map frame, to the right and centred vertically, so that it covers no county.
- `tm_borders()` adds a layer that draws only the county boundaries, here at half opacity
  (`col_alpha = 0.5`). `tm_polygons()` already draws the boundaries, in dark grey at full opacity,
  so on these maps the extra layer changes little. Chapter 9 includes the same layer.
- `tm_title()` adds the title above the map.
- `tmap_arrange()` places stored maps side by side in `ncol` columns. `asp = 1` gives each map an
  aspect ratio of 1, where the default, `0`, fits each map to its cell.
:::

In the chapters, the two maps illustrate the effect of the classification method on the apparent
pattern. With a right-skewed variable such as GDPPC, equal-interval breaks place most of the
province in the lowest class and Changsha alone in the highest. Quantile breaks assign an equal
number of counties to each class and show higher GDPPC in the north east than in the west.

Chapter 10 asks two questions of these maps:

- **Do they reveal outliers or clusters?** Changsha stands out as an outlier, the only county in the
  highest equal-interval class. The quantile map suggests a cluster of higher GDPPC in the north
  east and of lower GDPPC in the west.
- **Do they indicate hot spots or cold spots?** They suggest where these may lie, around Changsha
  and in the west, but a choropleth cannot show whether the pattern is significant. Section 3.3
  tests it for the province, and sections 4.1 and 4.2 for each county.

```{r}
summary(hunan$GDPPC)
```

## Contiguity weights

Chapter 9 builds the neighbour list with Queen contiguity and divides each county's weights by its
neighbour count. Exercise 4 built the same matrix.

```{r}
wm_q <- poly2nb(hunan, queen = TRUE)
summary(wm_q)
```

```{r}
rswm_q <- nb2listw(wm_q, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
rswm_q
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The two blocks above use two functions:

```r
poly2nb(pl, queen = TRUE)                                 # spdep
nb2listw(neighbours, style = "W", zero.policy = NULL)     # spdep
```

- `poly2nb()` builds a neighbour list from polygons: for each county, the row numbers of the
  counties whose boundaries touch it. With `queen = TRUE`, the default, one shared boundary point is
  enough, and `queen = FALSE` requires a shared edge. The call states the default, as chapter 9
  does.
- `nb2listw()` turns the neighbour list into a weights object, which the spdep tests take as their
  `listw` argument. `style = "W"`, the default, row-standardises the weights.
- `zero.policy = TRUE` allows a county with no neighbours. With the default, `NULL`, spdep uses its
  global option, under which a county with no neighbours stops the function with an error.

The figure follows one county, Anxiang in row 1, through the two functions. `poly2nb()` records
the row numbers of the five counties that touch it, and `nb2listw()` gives each of them a weight of
1/5.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.2
nb_ids <- c(1, wm_q[[1]])
nb_focus <- hunan |>
  mutate(row = row_number(),
         role = case_when(row == 1 ~ "Anxiang (row 1)",
                          row %in% wm_q[[1]] ~ "its neighbours",
                          TRUE ~ "other"),
         role = factor(role, levels = c("Anxiang (row 1)", "its neighbours", "other")))
nb_box <- st_bbox(st_buffer(st_union(nb_focus[nb_ids, ]), 5000))
nb_labels <- nb_focus[nb_ids, ] |>
  mutate(txt = paste0(row, "\n", NAME_3)) |>
  st_point_on_surface()

nb_map <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = nb_focus, aes(fill = role), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_sf_text(data = nb_labels, aes(label = txt), size = 2.8, lineheight = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Anxiang (row 1)" = "darkorange",
                               "its neighbours" = "#fdd49e", "other" = "grey90")) +
  coord_sf(xlim = nb_box[c("xmin", "xmax")], ylim = nb_box[c("ymin", "ymax")], datum = NA) +
  labs(fill = NULL, x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

nb_steps <- ggplot() +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0.95, label = "poly2nb()", family = "mono", size = 3.4, hjust = 0) +
  annotate("label", x = 0, y = 0.78, hjust = 0, family = "mono", size = 3.4,
           label = paste0("wm_q[[1]]\n", paste(wm_q[[1]], collapse = "    "))) +
  annotate("segment", x = 0.25, xend = 0.25, y = 0.64, yend = 0.46,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"))) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.3, y = 0.55, label = 'nb2listw(style = "W")',
           family = "mono", size = 3.4, hjust = 0) +
  annotate("label", x = 0, y = 0.3, hjust = 0, family = "mono", size = 3.4,
           label = paste0("rswm_q$weights[[1]]\n",
                          paste(rswm_q$weights[[1]], collapse = "  "))) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0.1, 1), clip = "off") +
  theme_void()

patchwork::wrap_plots(nb_map, nb_steps, widths = c(1.2, 1))
```
:::

Row standardisation makes each county's weights sum to 1. A lagged value is thus a weighted average
of the neighbouring values, on the same scale as the variable itself. Every global statistic below
is computed on this weights object.

## Moran's I

### The test

```{r}
moran.test(hunan$GDPPC,
           listw = rswm_q,
           zero.policy = TRUE,
           na.action = na.omit)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses one function:

```r
moran.test(x, listw, randomisation = TRUE, zero.policy = attr(listw, "zero.policy"),
           alternative = "greater", na.action = na.fail)                  # spdep
```

- `moran.test()` computes Moran's I for `x` with the weights in `listw`, and tests it against its
  expectation under spatial randomness. It reports I, its expectation and variance, and the
  z-score, labelled "standard deviate", with its p-value.
- `randomisation = TRUE`, the default, sets the null model for the variance of I. Section 5.5
  explains the choice.
- `alternative` sets the direction of the test. The three options are:

  | `alternative` | Tests whether I is | Pattern it looks for |
  |---|---|---|
  | `"greater"`, the default | above its expectation | clustering: neighbouring values tend to be similar |
  | `"less"` | below its expectation | dispersion: neighbouring values tend to be dissimilar |
  | `"two.sided"` | different from its expectation in either direction | either pattern |

  This page keeps the default, because the question is whether GDPPC clusters. `moran.mc()` in
  section 3.3.2 has the same default. The local statistics of Part 2 default to `"two.sided"`.
- `zero.policy = TRUE` permits counties with no neighbours. Hunan has no such county, so the
  argument has no effect here.
- `na.action = na.omit` drops counties with missing values, where the default, `na.fail`, stops
  with an error. GDPPC has no missing values, so this argument also has no effect.

The figure places the z-score of this test on the standard normal curve. The shaded bands mark how
far a z-score lies from zero, and the red line marks the result for GDPPC.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.6
z_obs <- unname(moran.test(hunan$GDPPC, listw = rswm_q, zero.policy = TRUE)$statistic)
cuts <- c(-Inf, -2.58, -1.96, -1.65, 1.65, 1.96, 2.58, Inf)
tibble(z = seq(-5.5, 5.5, 0.01), d = dnorm(z)) |>
  mutate(band = cut(z, cuts, labels = c("z < -2.58", "-2.58 to -1.96", "-1.96 to -1.65",
                                        "-1.65 to 1.65", "1.65 to 1.96", "1.96 to 2.58",
                                        "z > 2.58"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(z, d)) +
  geom_area(aes(fill = band, group = band)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = z_obs, colour = "darkred", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("label", x = z_obs, y = 0.2, hjust = 1.05, size = 3.2,
           label = paste0("GDPPC\nz = ", round(z_obs, 2))) +
  annotate("text", x = c(-3.8, 0, 3.8), y = 0.43, size = 3.5,
           label = c("Dispersed", "Random", "Clustered")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#2166ac", "#67a9cf", "#d1e5f0", "#fff7bc",
                               "#fddbc7", "#ef8a62", "#b2182b")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-2.58, -1.96, 0, 1.96, 2.58)) +
  labs(x = "z-score", y = NULL, fill = "z-score band") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```
:::

Chapter 9 asks what statistical conclusion the output supports:

- **Moran's I:** 0.301, against an expectation of −0.0115 under spatial randomness. The
  expectation, −1/(n−1), is slightly negative, because a county is not its own neighbour.
- **Test:** z = 4.74 and p = 1.1 × 10⁻⁶, so the null hypothesis of spatial randomness is rejected.

Slide 10 of the Lesson 5 lecture gives the reading of I, shown below on a scale from negative to
positive with the value for GDPPC marked.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 2.4
i_obs <- round(unname(moran.test(hunan$GDPPC, listw = rswm_q)$estimate[1]), 3)
ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -1, xmax = -0.1, ymin = -0.25, ymax = 0.25, fill = "#67a9cf", alpha = 0.5) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -0.1, xmax = 0.1, ymin = -0.25, ymax = 0.25, fill = "#fff7bc") +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0.1, xmax = 1, ymin = -0.25, ymax = 0.25, fill = "#ef8a62", alpha = 0.5) +
  annotate("segment", x = -1.05, xend = 1.08, y = 0, yend = 0, linewidth = 0.8,
           arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.3, "cm"))) +
  annotate("text", x = c(-0.55, 0, 0.55), y = 0.55, fontface = "bold", size = 4,
           label = c("Negative: dispersed", "About zero: random", "Positive: clustered")) +
  annotate("text", x = c(-0.55, 0, 0.55), y = -0.5, size = 3.2,
           label = c("neighbours tend to be dissimilar", "no spatial pattern",
                     "neighbours tend to be similar")) +
  annotate("point", x = i_obs, y = 0, size = 3.5, colour = "darkred") +
  annotate("label", x = i_obs, y = 0.25, vjust = -0.2, size = 3.2,
           label = paste0("GDPPC, I = ", i_obs)) +
  annotate("text", x = c(-1, 0, 1), y = -0.18, label = c("-1", "0", "+1"), size = 3) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-1.15, 1.15), ylim = c(-0.7, 0.75)) +
  theme_void()
```

The width of the middle band is schematic: whether a value of I is close enough to zero is decided
by the test above. GDPPC is in the positive case: counties have values more similar to those of
their neighbours than a random allocation of the same 88 values would produce. The test confirms
that the higher GDPPC in the north east and lower GDPPC in the west, shown by the quantile map in
section 3.1, is not an artefact of the visual interpretation of a choropleth.

### The permutation test

Moran's I has an analytical null distribution. It assumes either that the values are drawn from a
normal distribution or that they are a random permutation of the observed values. For a right-skewed
variable such as GDPPC, a test that does not depend on this assumption is preferable. A Monte Carlo
test constructs the null distribution empirically: the 88 values are randomly reassigned to the 88
counties many times, and I is computed for each permutation.

```{r}
set.seed(1234)
bperm <- moran.mc(hunan$GDPPC,
                  listw = rswm_q,
                  nsim = 999,
                  zero.policy = TRUE,
                  na.action = na.omit)
bperm
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses two functions:

```r
set.seed(seed)                                            # base R
moran.mc(x, listw, nsim, zero.policy = attr(listw, "zero.policy"),
         alternative = "greater", na.action = na.fail)    # spdep
```

- `set.seed()` fixes the starting point of R's random number generator. The permutations are then
  the same on every render, and the reported p-value does not change between renders.
- `moran.mc()` runs the Monte Carlo test: it reassigns the values of `x` to the counties at random
  `nsim` times and computes I for each assignment. `nsim` has no default. With `nsim = 999` the
  observed I is ranked among 1,000 values, so the smallest attainable pseudo p-value is 1/1000.
- `alternative = "greater"`, the default, tests for positive spatial autocorrelation. `na.action =
  na.omit` drops counties with missing values, where the default, `na.fail`, stops with an error.
  GDPPC has no missing values, so the argument has no effect here. `zero.policy` defaults to the
  setting stored in the weights object, and `rswm_q` was built with `zero.policy = TRUE`, so setting
  it again changes nothing.
- `bperm$res` holds the 999 simulated values followed by the observed I as its 1,000th element. The
  summaries and the histogram below use `bperm$res[1:999]`, which excludes the observed value.
  Chapter 9 plots the whole of `bperm$res`.
:::

Chapter 9 asks what statistical conclusion the output supports:

- **Rank:** the observed I ranks 1000th of 1000 values, above all 999 permuted values.
- **Pseudo p-value:** 0.001, the smallest attainable with 999 simulations.
- **Conclusion:** the null hypothesis of spatial randomness is rejected, as in section 3.3.1.

### The simulated distribution

```{r}
mean(bperm$res[1:999])
var(bperm$res[1:999])
summary(bperm$res[1:999])
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(tibble(I = bperm$res[1:999]), aes(x = I)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "grey70", colour = "black") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -1 / (nrow(hunan) - 1), colour = "red") +
  labs(x = "Simulated Moran's I", y = "Count",
       title = "Monte Carlo null distribution, 999 permutations") +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses these functions:

```r
tibble(...)                                               # tibble
ggplot(data, aes(x))                                      # ggplot2
geom_histogram(bins, fill, colour)                        # ggplot2
geom_vline(xintercept, colour)                            # ggplot2
labs(x, y, title)                                         # ggplot2
theme_minimal()                                           # ggplot2
```

- `tibble(I = bperm$res[1:999])` builds a data frame with one column, holding the 999 simulated
  values of Moran's I. The name `I` is chosen here and is only a column name.
- `ggplot()` starts a plot from that data frame. `aes()` sets the aesthetic mapping: which column
  controls which visual property of the plot, such as position, colour or size. `aes(x = I)` places
  the values of column `I` along the horizontal axis. The observed I is not among them, and the text
  below the plot compares it with the simulated values.
- Each `+` adds a layer or a setting. `geom_histogram()` sorts the values into `bins = 20` intervals
  and draws a bar for each, with `fill` setting the colour of the bars and `colour` their outline.
- `geom_vline()` draws a vertical line at `xintercept`, here the expectation −1/(n−1).
- `labs()` sets the axis labels and the title, and `theme_minimal()` removes the grey background.
:::

Chapter 9 asks what statistical observation the histogram supports:

- **Centre:** the simulated values are distributed approximately symmetrically around the
  expectation −1/(n−1), marked by the red line. Chapter 9 draws the line at zero, which at n = 88 is
  0.0115 away and indistinguishable on this axis.
- **Observed value:** 0.301, beyond the largest of the 999 simulated values, 0.276.

Chapter 9 also sets a challenge: to plot the values with `ggplot2` instead of base graphics. The
histogram above is drawn with `ggplot2`.

## Geary's C

### The test

Moran's I is based on the deviation of each county from the provincial mean. Geary's C is based on
the squared differences between each county and its neighbours, so it is more sensitive to local
differences between neighbouring values.

```{r}
geary.test(hunan$GDPPC, listw = rswm_q)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses one function:

```r
geary.test(x, listw, randomisation = TRUE, zero.policy = attr(listw, "zero.policy"),
           alternative = "greater")                                        # spdep
```

- `geary.test()` computes Geary's C for `x` with the weights in `listw`, and tests it against its
  expectation of 1 under spatial randomness. The call passes only `x` and `listw`, so every other
  argument keeps its default.
- The "standard deviate" in the output is (1 − C) divided by the standard deviation of C, so it is
  positive when C is below 1. `alternative = "greater"` therefore tests for clustering, as it does
  for Moran's I, although clustering makes C smaller than its expectation.
- `randomisation = TRUE`, the default, sets the null model for the variance of C, as for
  `moran.test()` in section 3.3.1.

The two maps compare the statistics on one county, Anxiang, and its five neighbours from section
3.2. Moran's I compares every county with the provincial mean. Geary's C compares Anxiang directly
with each neighbour and squares the difference, so the mean plays no part.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.6
mc_mu <- mean(hunan$GDPPC)
mc_pts <- st_point_on_surface(nb_focus[nb_ids, ]) |>
  mutate(dev = GDPPC - mc_mu, diff = GDPPC[1] - GDPPC)
mc_xy <- st_coordinates(mc_pts)
mc_links <- tibble(x = mc_xy[1, 1], y = mc_xy[1, 2], xend = mc_xy[-1, 1], yend = mc_xy[-1, 2],
                   diff = mc_pts$diff[-1], name = mc_pts$NAME_3[-1])
fmt <- function(v) paste0(ifelse(v > 0, "+", ""), format(round(v), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE))
zoom <- coord_sf(xlim = nb_box[c("xmin", "xmax")], ylim = nb_box[c("ymin", "ymax")], datum = NA)

moran_view <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = nb_focus, fill = "grey92", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_sf(data = mutate(nb_focus[nb_ids, ], dev = GDPPC - mc_mu), aes(fill = dev),
          colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_sf_text(data = mc_pts, aes(label = paste0(NAME_3, "\n", fmt(dev))), size = 2.8,
               lineheight = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b", midpoint = 0,
                       guide = "none") +
  zoom +
  labs(title = "Moran's I: each county against the mean",
       subtitle = paste0("deviation from the provincial mean of ",
                         format(round(mc_mu), big.mark = ","))) +
  theme_void()

geary_view <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = nb_focus, aes(fill = role), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_segment(data = mc_links, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend), colour = "grey30") +
  geom_label(data = mc_links, aes(x = x + 0.7 * (xend - x), y = y + 0.7 * (yend - y),
                 label = paste0(name, ": ", format(abs(diff), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE))),
             size = 2.6, label.size = 0, fill = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Anxiang (row 1)" = "darkorange",
                               "its neighbours" = "#fdd49e", "other" = "grey92"),
                    guide = "none") +
  zoom +
  labs(title = "Geary's C: Anxiang against each neighbour",
       subtitle = "size of the difference in GDPPC, which C squares") +
  theme_void()

patchwork::wrap_plots(moran_view, geary_view, ncol = 2)
```
:::

Chapter 9 asks what statistical conclusion the output supports. Geary's C for GDPPC is 0.691,
against an expectation of exactly 1 (z = 3.61, p = 1.5 × 10⁻⁴), so the null hypothesis of spatial
randomness is rejected.

Its scale is inverted relative to Moran's I. Slide 12 of the Lesson 5 lecture states that C
approaches 0 and I approaches 1 when similar values cluster:

| Pattern | Moran's I | Geary's C |
|---|---|---|
| clustered: neighbouring values similar | positive, towards 1 | below 1, towards 0 |
| random | about its expectation, −0.0115 | about 1 |
| dispersed: neighbouring values dissimilar | negative | above 1 |
| **GDPPC** | **0.301** | **0.691** |

Both values are on the clustered side, so like Moran's I, C indicates significant positive spatial
autocorrelation.

### The permutation test

```{r}
set.seed(1234)
bperm <- geary.mc(hunan$GDPPC,
                  listw = rswm_q,
                  nsim = 999)
bperm
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses one function:

```r
geary.mc(x, listw, nsim, zero.policy = attr(listw, "zero.policy"),
         alternative = "greater")                                          # spdep
```

- `geary.mc()` runs the Monte Carlo test for Geary's C in the same way as `moran.mc()` in section
  3.3.2: it reassigns the values of `x` to the counties at random `nsim` times and computes C for
  each assignment. `set.seed(1234)` again makes the permutations the same on every render.
- With `alternative = "greater"`, the pseudo p-value counts the permuted values of C that are at or
  below the observed one, since a small C indicates clustering.
- The result is stored in `bperm`, which replaces the Moran's I result of section 3.3.2. As before,
  `bperm$res` holds the 999 simulated values followed by the observed C as its 1,000th element.
:::

Chapter 9 asks what statistical conclusion the output supports:

- **Rank:** the observed C, 0.69072, ranks first of the 1000 values, below all 999 permuted values.
- **Pseudo p-value:** 0.001, the smallest attainable with 999 simulations.
- **Conclusion:** the null hypothesis of spatial randomness is rejected, as in section 3.4.1.

### The simulated distribution

```{r}
mean(bperm$res[1:999])
var(bperm$res[1:999])
summary(bperm$res[1:999])
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(tibble(C = bperm$res[1:999]), aes(x = C)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "grey70", colour = "black") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "red") +
  labs(x = "Simulated Geary's C", y = "Count",
       title = "Monte Carlo null distribution, 999 permutations") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Chapter 9 asks what statistical observation the histogram supports:

- **Centre:** the reference line at 1 is the expectation under spatial randomness, and the simulated
  mean is approximately equal to it.
- **Observed value:** 0.691 lies beyond the left tail, which for Geary's C is the side that
  indicates clustering.

## Spatial correlogram

Both statistics so far were computed on first-order neighbours only. A spatial correlogram computes
the statistic at successive lag orders, where lag 2 comprises the neighbours of the neighbours, and
shows the range of lags over which spatial autocorrelation persists.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
MI_corr <- sp.correlogram(wm_q,
                          hunan$GDPPC,
                          order = 6,
                          method = "I",
                          style = "W")
plot(MI_corr)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses one function:

```r
sp.correlogram(neighbours, var, order = 1, method = "corr", style = "W")   # spdep
```

- `sp.correlogram()` computes a spatial autocorrelation statistic at each lag from 1 to `order`. It
  takes the neighbour list `wm_q` because it builds the higher-order neighbours itself, so it needs
  no weights object. The lag-2 neighbours of a county are the neighbours of its neighbours,
  excluding the county itself and its lag-1 neighbours, and so on up to `order = 6`.
- `method` selects the statistic. The default, `"corr"`, is a correlation coefficient, so
  `method = "I"` is needed for Moran's I. The Geary correlogram below uses `method = "C"`.
- `style = "W"` row-standardises the weights at each lag. `plot()` draws the value at each lag with
  a bar two standard deviations either side, and a horizontal line at the expected value under
  spatial randomness.

The map shows the lags that `sp.correlogram()` builds, counted from one county, Changsha. Each
county is coloured by the number of steps across shared boundaries that separate it from Changsha.
At lag 1 Changsha is compared with its immediate neighbours, and at lags 5 and 6 with counties in the
west and south of the province.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 5.5
cs <- which(hunan$NAME_3 == "Changsha")
lags <- nblag(wm_q, 6)
lag_order <- rep(NA_integer_, nrow(hunan))
for (k in 1:6) lag_order[lags[[k]][[cs]]] <- k
lag_order[cs] <- 0L

hunan |>
  mutate(lag = factor(ifelse(is.na(lag_order), "beyond 6", as.character(lag_order)),
                      levels = c(as.character(0:6), "beyond 6"),
                      labels = c("Changsha", paste("lag", 1:6), "beyond lag 6"))) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = lag), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("black", "#08306b", "#2171b5", "#6baed6",
                               "#c6dbef", "#fdd0a2", "#fd8d3c", "grey85")) +
  labs(fill = "Steps from Changsha") +
  theme_void()
```
:::

```{r}
print(MI_corr)
```

Chapter 9 asks what statistical observation the correlogram supports:

- **Decline:** Moran's I falls from 0.30 at lag 1 to 0.03 at lag 4.
- **Sign change:** it turns negative between lags 4 and 5, and is significantly negative at lags 5
  and 6.
- **Reason:** negative values at the higher lags reflect the geometry of the province as well as the
  distribution of GDPPC. At lag 5 the neighbour sets of a county extend across the province.
  Counties in the north east are then compared with counties in the west, and the values at the two
  ends differ.

Lag 4 is the first order at which the null hypothesis of no spatial autocorrelation is not rejected.
Lag 3 is significant at p = 0.04, a marginal result that warrants adjustment, since six tests are
reported in one table. A correction raises the evidence a test must reach, so that a lag counts as
significant only on stronger evidence than 0.05. Holm's correction ranks the six p-values and
applies the strictest threshold to the smallest, then a looser threshold to each in turn.
`print.spcor()` defaults to `p.adj.method = "none"`, so the first table reported unadjusted
p-values.

```{r}
print(MI_corr, p.adj.method = "holm")
```

Under Holm's correction lag 3 is no longer significant (p = 0.081), and the p-value at lag 6
increases to 0.027. At lags 1, 2 and 5 the p-values all increase and all remain below 0.001. Only
lag 4 is unchanged, since it already had the largest p-value in the table. Section 5.3 addresses the
same multiple-comparisons problem on a much larger scale, for the 88 local statistics.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
GC_corr <- sp.correlogram(wm_q,
                          hunan$GDPPC,
                          order = 6,
                          method = "C",
                          style = "W")
plot(GC_corr)
```

```{r}
print(GC_corr)
```

Geary's C increases from 0.69 towards 1 and then exceeds it. Its correlogram has the shape of the
Moran correlogram with the vertical axis reversed. Their p-values, however, do not follow the same
pattern.

| Lag | Moran p | Geary p |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2.2e-06 | 3.1e-04 |
| 2 | 2.0e-06 | 7.2e-04 |
| 3 | 0.040 | 0.389 |
| 4 | 0.226 | 0.876 |
| 5 | 6.0e-05 | 7.6e-04 |
| 6 | 0.0089 | 0.310 |

Moran's I and Geary's C agree at lags 1, 2, 4 and 5. At lags 3 and 6 Moran's I is significant and
Geary's C is not. This difference follows from the structure of the two statistics. Moran's I is
based on deviations from the provincial mean, and a gradual trend across the province contributes to
it. Geary's C is based on differences between neighbouring values, and a weak trend that leaves
adjacent pairs similar contributes little to it. Section 5.6 finds the opposite for the local forms:
local Geary's c identifies more significant counties than local Moran's I, 21 against 16.

# Part 2: Local measures of spatial autocorrelation

This part follows r4gdsa [Chapter 10](https://r4gdsa.netlify.app/chap10.html). Each statistic in it
is computed for every county, and the results are mapped. Chapter 10 repeats the data import and the
GDPPC maps of chapter 9, which are in sections 2 and 3.1 of this page and are not repeated here.

## Local indicators of spatial association

A global statistic summarises the whole province in a single value. It shows neither where the
clustering is concentrated nor which individual counties differ from their neighbours. A local
indicator of spatial association (LISA) is computed for each county and answers both questions.
Anselin (1995) defines a LISA as any statistic that satisfies two requirements:

1. **Local clustering.** It "gives an indication of the extent of significant spatial clustering of
   similar values around that observation".
2. **Link to the global statistic.** "The sum of LISAs for all observations is proportional to a
   global indicator of spatial association".

Local Moran's I satisfies both. Under the second requirement, its 88 local values sum to a quantity
proportional to the global Moran's I of section 3.3, as slide 22 of the Lesson 5 lecture shows.

### Weights the sfdep way

`sfdep` stores the neighbour list and the weights as columns of the sf object, each holding a list.
Each row holds a county's geometry, its attributes, its neighbours and its weights.

```{r}
wm_q <- hunan |>
  mutate(nb = st_contiguity(geometry),
         wt = st_weights(nb, style = "W"),
         .before = 1)
summary(wm_q$nb)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses three functions:

```r
mutate(.data, name = value, ..., .before = NULL)          # dplyr
st_contiguity(geometry, queen = TRUE)                     # sfdep
st_weights(nb, style = "W", allow_zero = NULL)            # sfdep
```

- `mutate()` adds columns to a data frame. Each `name = value` pair creates one column, here `nb`
  and `wt`. A later pair can use a column created by an earlier one, so `wt` is computed from the
  `nb` created on the line above.
- `.before` sets where the new columns go, and takes a column position or a column name. `.before =
  1` places them before the column now in position 1, so they become the first two columns. The
  default, `NULL`, adds them after the existing columns. Placing them first makes them visible at
  the start of each printed row.
- `st_contiguity()` finds, for each polygon, the polygons that share a boundary with it, and returns
  a neighbour list: for each county, a vector of the row numbers of its neighbours. With `queen =
  TRUE`, the default, a single shared boundary point is enough. `queen = FALSE` requires a shared
  edge. The function calls `poly2nb()` from section 3.2, so it returns the same list.
- `st_weights()` gives each neighbour a weight. With `style = "W"`, the default, each of a county's
  weights is 1 divided by its number of neighbours, so its weights sum to 1. The function calls
  `nb2listw()` from section 3.2 and keeps only the weights. `allow_zero` concerns counties without
  neighbours, and Hunan has none.

### Local Moran's I

```{r}
set.seed(1234)
lisa <- wm_q |>
  mutate(local_moran = local_moran(GDPPC, nb, wt, nsim = 999),
         .before = 1) |>
  unnest(local_moran)
glimpse(lisa)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses three functions:

```r
local_moran(x, nb, wt, alternative = "two.sided", nsim = 499)   # sfdep
unnest(data, cols)                                              # tidyr
glimpse(x)                                                      # dplyr
```

- `local_moran()` computes local Moran's I for each county and tests it by conditional permutation.
  It returns a data frame with one row per county and one column per result. `nsim` defaults to
  499, and the call sets 999 to match section 3.3.2. With `alternative = "two.sided"`, the default,
  both unusually high and unusually low values of Ii count as significant.
- Inside `mutate()` (section 4.1.1), that data frame is stored as a single column named
  `local_moran`, and `.before = 1` places it first.
- `unnest()` replaces the column named in `cols` with the columns it contains, so the 12 results
  become 12 columns.
- `glimpse()` prints the name, type and first values of every column, one column per line.

Before `unnest()`, `local_moran` is a single column that holds a 12-column data frame, one row per
county:

The values shown are those of the first two counties, Anxiang and Hanshou.
:::

Section 5.2 compares two of these p-value columns, `p_ii` and `p_ii_sim`. Each column is described
below.

| Column | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `ii` | the local Moran's I value for that county |
| `eii`, `var_ii`, `z_ii` | the permutation sample mean, variance and standardised deviate. With `nsim` supplied these are computed from the simulations, not from the analytical null |
| `p_ii` | a p-value from `pnorm()` on `z_ii`, so a normal approximation to the permutation distribution |
| `p_ii_sim` | a rank-based p-value from the same permutations, two-sided, on a [0, 1] scale |
| `p_folded_sim` | the same ranking folded onto a [0, 1] range of 0.5, so close to half of `p_ii_sim` |
| `mean`, `median`, `pysal` | three labellings of the county into one of the four scatterplot quadrants |

Under the analytical randomisation null hypothesis with row-standardised weights, every county has
the same expectation, −1/(n−1) = −0.0115. The printed values of `eii` differ between counties, so
they are sample means over the permutations.

Chapter 10 uses `p_ii`. This page uses `p_ii_sim`, for the reasons given in section 5.2.

### The two maps

```{r}
#| fig-height: 10.13
tm_shape(lisa) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "ii",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "pretty", n = 5,
                                              values = "brewer.rd_bu"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Local Moran's I",
                                      position = tm_pos_out())) +
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Local Moran's I of GDPPC, Queen contiguity")
```

A large positive value indicates a county whose neighbours have similar values. A negative value
indicates a county whose value differs from those of its neighbours. On its own, Ii does not
indicate whether the association is significant. The p-value map below provides that information.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 10.13
tm_shape(lisa) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "p_ii_sim",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 1),
                values = "-brewer.reds"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "simulated p-value",
                                      position = tm_pos_out())) +
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Simulated p-values of local Moran's I, 999 permutations")
```

```{r}
min(lisa$p_ii_sim)
```

The legend breaks differ from those of the chapter. `p_ii_sim` is a rank-based p-value, and its
smallest attainable value is `2 / (nsim + 1)`, which is 0.002 at `nsim = 999` and 0.02 at the
chapter's `nsim = 99`. The breaks are set at values attainable with `nsim = 999` (section 5.2).

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.1
ii.map <- tm_shape(lisa) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "ii",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "pretty", n = 5,
                                              values = "brewer.rd_bu"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Local Moran's I",
                                      position = tm_pos_out("right", "center"))) +
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Local Moran's I")

p_ii.map <- tm_shape(lisa) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "p_ii_sim",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 1),
                values = "-brewer.reds"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "p-value",
                                      position = tm_pos_out("right", "center"))) +
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Simulated p-value")

tmap_arrange(ii.map, p_ii.map, asp = 1, ncol = 2)
```

Neither map is sufficient on its own. Several counties with a large value of `ii` are not
significant, and the set of significant counties is smaller than the set of counties with prominent
values on the first map.

### Moran scatterplot

```{r}
lisa <- lisa |>
  mutate(lag_GDPPC = st_lag(GDPPC, nb, wt), .before = 1)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses one function:

```r
st_lag(x, nb, wt)                                         # sfdep
```

- `st_lag()` computes the spatial lag of `x`: for each county, the sum of its neighbours' values,
  each multiplied by its weight. With row-standardised weights this is the average GDPPC of the
  neighbours, which the scatterplot below plots against the county's own GDPPC.

The figure works through the lag for Anxiang. Each of its five neighbours has a weight of 0.2, so
its lag is the average GDPPC of the five.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.4
lag_ids <- wm_q$nb[[1]]
lag_labels <- nb_focus[c(1, lag_ids), ] |>
  mutate(txt = paste0(NAME_3, "\n", format(GDPPC, big.mark = ","))) |>
  st_point_on_surface()
lag_map <- nb_map
lag_map$layers[[2]] <- geom_sf_text(data = lag_labels, aes(label = txt), size = 2.8,
                                    lineheight = 0.9)

terms <- paste0(c("  ", rep("+ ", length(lag_ids) - 1)),
                format(wm_q$wt[[1]], nsmall = 1), " x ",
                format(hunan$GDPPC[lag_ids], big.mark = ","),
                "  (", hunan$NAME_3[lag_ids], ")")
lag_lines <- c("st_lag(GDPPC, nb, wt), row 1:", "",
               "lag = sum of weight x neighbour GDPPC", "", terms, "",
               paste0("= ", format(round(lisa$lag_GDPPC[1], 1), big.mark = ",")),
               "", paste0("Anxiang's own GDPPC: ", format(hunan$GDPPC[1], big.mark = ",")))
lag_steps <- ggplot() +
  annotate("segment", x = -0.12, xend = -0.02, y = 0.5, yend = 0.5,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"))) +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0.5, hjust = 0, vjust = 0.5, family = "mono", size = 3.1,
           lineheight = 1.05, label = paste(lag_lines, collapse = "\n")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.15, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), clip = "off") +
  theme_void()

patchwork::wrap_plots(lag_map, lag_steps, widths = c(1.2, 1))
```
:::

```{r}
#| fig-height: 6
ggplot(data = lisa, aes(x = GDPPC, y = lag_GDPPC)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "red") +
  labs(x = "GDPPC",
       y = "Spatial lag of GDPPC",
       title = "Moran scatterplot") +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses two new functions:

```r
geom_point(size)                                          # ggplot2
geom_smooth(method = NULL, se = TRUE, colour)             # ggplot2
```

- `aes(x = GDPPC, y = lag_GDPPC)` places each county's GDPPC on the horizontal axis and its spatial
  lag on the vertical axis.
- `geom_point()` draws one point per county.
- `geom_smooth()` adds a fitted line. `method = "lm"` fits a straight line by least squares, and
  `se = FALSE` leaves out the grey confidence band that is drawn by default.
:::

This is the scatterplot from the end of Hands-on Exercise 4, with a fitted regression line added.
With row-standardised weights, Moran's I is the least-squares slope of the spatial lag on the
variable in deviations from its mean. Anselin (1996) writes I = y'Wy / y'y and treats the plot as
the regression of Wy on y. The slope of the line above is therefore Moran's I.

Anselin (1996) standardises the variable and then takes the spatial lag of the standardised values,
so the vertical axis is Wz. Chapter 10 standardises the lag separately, with `scale(lag_GDPPC)`.
This page follows Anselin (1996):

```{r}
lisa <- lisa |>
  mutate(z_GDPPC = as.numeric(scale(GDPPC)),
         z_lag_GDPPC = st_lag(z_GDPPC, nb, wt),
         .before = 1)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses two functions:

```r
scale(x, center = TRUE, scale = TRUE)                     # base R
as.numeric(x)                                             # base R
```

- `scale()` standardises a variable: it subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation, so
  the result has mean 0 and standard deviation 1.
- `scale()` returns an 88 × 1 matrix, and `as.numeric()` turns it back into a plain vector, so that
  it can be stored as an ordinary column.
- `st_lag()` then takes the spatial lag of the standardised values, which is Anselin's (1996)
  construction.
:::

The two constructions, the lag of the standardised variable and the separately standardised lag,
give different slopes on the same 88 counties:

```{r}
tibble(construction = c("Moran's I (section 3.3.1)",
                        "lag of GDPPC on GDPPC",
                        "Anselin (1996): lag of z on z",
                        "chapter 10: scale(lag) on z"),
       slope = c(moran.test(hunan$GDPPC, rswm_q)$estimate[1],
                 coef(lm(lag_GDPPC ~ GDPPC, data = lisa))[2],
                 coef(lm(z_lag_GDPPC ~ z_GDPPC, data = lisa))[2],
                 coef(lm(as.numeric(scale(lag_GDPPC)) ~ z_GDPPC, data = lisa))[2])) |>
  kable(digits = 4)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses three new functions:

```r
lm(formula, data)                                         # stats
coef(object)                                              # stats
kable(x, digits)                                          # knitr
```

- `lm()` fits a linear regression. The formula `lag_GDPPC ~ GDPPC` reads "lag_GDPPC explained by
  GDPPC": the variable before `~` is on the vertical axis of the scatterplot and the one after it on
  the horizontal axis.
- `coef()` returns the fitted coefficients, the intercept first and the slope second, so `[2]`
  takes the slope.
- `kable()` prints a data frame as a formatted table, and `digits = 4` rounds the numbers to four
  decimal places.
:::

The chapter's figure is titled a Moran scatterplot, but its regression line does not have Moran's I
as its slope. Under the chapter's construction the slope is 0.485, the Pearson correlation between
GDPPC and its spatial lag. The lag is an average of neighbouring values and varies less than GDPPC
(standard deviations of about 9,300 and 15,000 yuan), so standardising it by its own standard
deviation stretches it. Under Anselin's (1996) construction the slope is 0.301, equal to Moran's I.
The assignment of counties to quadrants is the same under both constructions for this data.


```{r}
#| fig-height: 6
ggplot(data = lisa, aes(x = z_GDPPC, y = z_lag_GDPPC, colour = mean)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "black") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, lty = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, lty = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("High-High" = "red",
                                 "Low-Low" = "blue",
                                 "Low-High" = "lightblue",
                                 "High-Low" = "pink")) +
  labs(x = "Standardised GDPPC",
       y = "Standardised spatial lag of GDPPC",
       colour = "Quadrant",
       title = "Standardised Moran scatterplot with LISA quadrants") +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses two new functions:

```r
geom_hline(yintercept, lty)                               # ggplot2
scale_colour_manual(values)                               # ggplot2
```

- `colour = mean` inside `aes()` colours each point by its quadrant label in the `mean` column.
- `geom_hline()` and `geom_vline()` (section 3.3.3) draw the dashed lines at zero, and `lty = 2`
  sets a dashed line.
- `scale_colour_manual()` sets the colour of each quadrant by name, matching the colours of the
  LISA cluster map in section 4.1.5.
:::

The dashed lines mark zero, the mean of a standardised variable.

In the LISA cluster map, counties are classified by the four quadrants:

| Quadrant | Position | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| High-High | top right | a high value surrounded by high values, the core of a cluster |
| Low-Low | bottom left | a low value surrounded by low values |
| High-Low | bottom right | a high value surrounded by low values, a spatial outlier |
| Low-High | top left | a low value surrounded by high values, a spatial outlier |

Counties in the High-High and Low-Low quadrants have a positive local I, and counties in the
High-Low and Low-High quadrants have a negative local I. The sign of Ii alone does not identify the
quadrant: a positive value may indicate a High-High or a Low-Low cluster, and a negative value a
High-Low or a Low-High outlier (Anselin 1995).

### LISA cluster map

```{r}
signif <- 0.05

lisa <- lisa |>
  mutate(LISA_cluster = ifelse(p_ii_sim < signif, as.character(mean), "Insignificant"),
         LISA_cluster = factor(LISA_cluster,
                               levels = c("Insignificant", "Low-Low", "Low-High",
                                          "High-Low", "High-High")))
table(lisa$LISA_cluster)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses three functions:

```r
ifelse(test, yes, no)                                     # base R
as.character(x)                                           # base R
factor(x, levels)                                         # base R
```

- `signif <- 0.05` stores the significance threshold once. The hot and cold spot classification in
  section 4.2.3 uses it again.
- `ifelse()` works element by element: for each county it returns `yes` where `test` is true and
  `no` where it is false. A significant county takes its quadrant label from the `mean` column, and
  the others are labelled "Insignificant".
- `as.character()` converts the factor `mean` to its text labels. Without it, `ifelse()` would
  return the factor's integer codes.
- The second line of `mutate()` (section 4.1.1) overwrites the column created on the first.
  `factor()` converts the labels to a factor, and `levels` fixes the order of its five classes. The
  paragraph after the map gives the reason. `table()` counts the counties in each class.

A factor stores a set of labels as numbers, together with an ordered list of the labels, called its
levels. The example follows four counties through the second line of `mutate()`:

<div style="display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 1em; flex-wrap: wrap;">
<div>After <code>ifelse()</code>: text<br><table class="table table-sm" style="width: auto; margin: 0;"><tr><th>County</th><th>LISA_cluster</th></tr><tr><td>Anxiang</td><td>Insignificant</td></tr><tr><td>Yuanling</td><td>Low-Low</td></tr><tr><td>Pingjiang</td><td>Low-High</td></tr><tr><td>Liuyang</td><td>High-High</td></tr></table></div>
<div style="font-size: 1.8em;">&rarr;</div>
<div>After <code>factor(levels = ...)</code><br><table class="table table-sm" style="width: auto; margin: 0;"><tr><th>County</th><th style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">stored as</th><th>shown as</th></tr><tr><td>Anxiang</td><td style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">1</td><td>Insignificant</td></tr><tr><td>Yuanling</td><td style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">2</td><td>Low-Low</td></tr><tr><td>Pingjiang</td><td style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">3</td><td>Low-High</td></tr><tr><td>Liuyang</td><td style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">5</td><td>High-High</td></tr></table></div>
<div>Its levels, in order<br><table class="table table-sm" style="width: auto; margin: 0;"><tr><th style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">level</th><th>label</th></tr><tr><td style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">1</td><td>Insignificant</td></tr><tr><td style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">2</td><td>Low-Low</td></tr><tr><td style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">3</td><td>Low-High</td></tr><tr><td style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">4</td><td>High-Low</td></tr><tr><td style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">5</td><td>High-High</td></tr></table></div>
</div>

Each county is stored as the number of its level, and the label is shown in its place. The order of
the levels decides the order of the classes in `table()`, in the legend and in the colours of the
map. High-Low is level 4 although no county has it, so it keeps its place in that order.
:::

```{r}
#| fig-height: 10.13
tm_shape(lisa) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "LISA_cluster",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
                values = c("grey80", "blue", "lightblue", "pink", "red")),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "LISA cluster",
                                      position = tm_pos_out("right", "center"))) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_title("Local Moran's I clusters of GDPPC, p < 0.05")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses one new function:

```r
tm_scale_categorical(values = NA, levels.drop = FALSE)    # tmap
```

- `tm_scale_categorical()` gives each category of a factor its own colour, in the order of the
  factor's levels. The vector of colours has to be written in the same order as the `levels`
  argument of section 4.1.5's `factor()` call, and the levels are set explicitly for that reason.
- `levels.drop = FALSE`, the default, keeps a level in the legend even when no county has it, so the
  colours stay fixed.

The colours are matched to the levels by position. With the levels set in section 4.1.5, each
class gets its intended colour. Without them, R sorts the classes alphabetically and drops High-Low,
which no county has, so the same five colours are matched to four levels in a different order:

<div style="display: flex; align-items: flex-start; gap: 1.5em; flex-wrap: wrap;">
<div>Levels set in section 4.1.5<br><table class="table table-sm" style="width: auto; margin: 0;"><tr><th>Level, in order</th><th>Counties</th><th>Colour given</th></tr><tr><td>Insignificant</td><td>72</td><td><span style="display:inline-block;width:1em;height:1em;vertical-align:middle;border:1px solid #999;background:#CCCCCC"></span> grey80</td></tr><tr><td>Low-Low</td><td>9</td><td><span style="display:inline-block;width:1em;height:1em;vertical-align:middle;border:1px solid #999;background:#0000FF"></span> blue</td></tr><tr><td>Low-High</td><td>1</td><td><span style="display:inline-block;width:1em;height:1em;vertical-align:middle;border:1px solid #999;background:#ADD8E6"></span> lightblue</td></tr><tr><td>High-Low</td><td>0</td><td><span style="display:inline-block;width:1em;height:1em;vertical-align:middle;border:1px solid #999;background:#FFC0CB"></span> pink</td></tr><tr><td>High-High</td><td>6</td><td><span style="display:inline-block;width:1em;height:1em;vertical-align:middle;border:1px solid #999;background:#FF0000"></span> red</td></tr></table></div>
<div>Levels left to R, alphabetical<br><table class="table table-sm" style="width: auto; margin: 0;"><tr><th>Level, in order</th><th>Counties</th><th>Colour given</th></tr><tr><td>High-High</td><td>6</td><td><span style="display:inline-block;width:1em;height:1em;vertical-align:middle;border:1px solid #999;background:#CCCCCC"></span> grey80</td></tr><tr><td>Insignificant</td><td>72</td><td><span style="display:inline-block;width:1em;height:1em;vertical-align:middle;border:1px solid #999;background:#0000FF"></span> blue</td></tr><tr><td>Low-High</td><td>1</td><td><span style="display:inline-block;width:1em;height:1em;vertical-align:middle;border:1px solid #999;background:#ADD8E6"></span> lightblue</td></tr><tr><td>Low-Low</td><td>9</td><td><span style="display:inline-block;width:1em;height:1em;vertical-align:middle;border:1px solid #999;background:#FFC0CB"></span> pink</td></tr></table></div>
</div>

In the second case the six High-High counties would be drawn grey and the 72 insignificant counties
blue.
:::

Chapter 10 asks what statistical observations the LISA map supports:

- **Significant counties:** 16 of the 88, of which six are High-High, nine Low-Low and one
  Low-High. The other 72 are not significant at p < 0.05.
- **High-High cluster:** around Changsha in the north east.
- **Low-Low cluster:** in the west.
- **Spatial outlier:** Pingjiang, the single Low-High county, which lies between the two groups and
  has low GDPPC with high-GDPPC neighbours.

These are uncorrected results. Section 5.3 shows how many remain significant after a correction
for 88 tests.

## Hot and cold spots

Local Moran's I and Getis-Ord Gi\* measure different concepts of spatial association.

| Statistic | What it measures | Significant positive value | Significant negative value |
|---|---|---|---|
| local Moran's I | similarity between a county and its neighbours | the county is similar to its neighbours, High-High or Low-Low | a spatial outlier, High-Low or Low-High |
| Gi\* | whether the sum of values in the neighbourhood is larger or smaller than expected under spatial randomness | clustering of high values, a hot spot | clustering of low values, a cold spot |

Gi\* has no outlier category.

Getis and Ord (1992) state that the variable "has a natural origin and is positive", because G is
computed from the values themselves and not from their deviations from the mean, so a zero that does
not represent absence of the quantity changes the statistic (section 5.4.1). GDPPC is positive in
every county.

### Distance weights

Getis and Ord (1992) define Gi\* on a distance band: it measures the concentration of values within
a given distance of each county. Slide 36 of the Lesson 5 lecture requires the band to be wide
enough that every county has at least one neighbour.

```{r}
ct <- critical_threshold(st_geometry(hunan))
ct
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses two functions:

```r
st_geometry(x)                                            # sf
critical_threshold(geometry, k = 1)                       # sfdep
```

- `st_geometry()` extracts the geometry column of an sf object, without the attributes.
- `critical_threshold()` finds each county's distance to its nearest neighbour (`k = 1`) and
  returns the largest of these distances. A distance band of that width gives every county at least
  one neighbour. The distance is in metres, because `hunan` is in EPSG:32649.

`st_geometry(hunan)` keeps only the shaded column, the polygons:

<div style="display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 1em; flex-wrap: wrap;">
<div><code>hunan</code>, an sf data frame<br><table class="table table-sm" style="width: auto; margin: 0;"><tr><th>NAME_2</th><th>ID_3</th><th>NAME_3</th><th>ENGTYPE_3</th><th>County</th><th>GDPPC</th><th style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">geometry</th></tr><tr><td>Changde</td><td>21098</td><td>Anxiang</td><td>County</td><td>Anxiang</td><td>23667</td><td style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">POLYGON ((602726.4 3292136, …))</td></tr><tr><td>Changde</td><td>21100</td><td>Hanshou</td><td>County</td><td>Hanshou</td><td>20981</td><td style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">POLYGON ((619553.5 3221554, …))</td></tr><tr><td>…</td><td>…</td><td>…</td><td>…</td><td>…</td><td>…</td><td style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">…</td></tr></table></div>
<div style="font-size: 1.8em;">&rarr;</div>
<div><code>st_geometry(hunan)</code>, an <code>sfc_POLYGON</code><br><table class="table table-sm" style="width: auto; margin: 0;"><tr><th style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">geometry</th></tr><tr><td style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">POLYGON ((602726.4 3292136, …))</td></tr><tr><td style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">POLYGON ((619553.5 3221554, …))</td></tr><tr><td style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">…</td></tr></table></div>
</div>

The result has no attributes, so `critical_threshold()` receives only the 88 shapes it measures.

The figure draws, for every county, a line to its nearest neighbour. The longest of these lines,
in red, is the value `critical_threshold()` returns.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 5
ct_pts <- st_point_on_surface(st_geometry(hunan))
ct_nn <- knearneigh(ct_pts, k = 1)$nn[, 1]
ct_xy <- st_coordinates(ct_pts)
ct_links <- tibble(x = ct_xy[, 1], y = ct_xy[, 2],
                   xend = ct_xy[ct_nn, 1], yend = ct_xy[ct_nn, 2]) |>
  mutate(d = sqrt((xend - x)^2 + (yend - y)^2))
far <- which.max(ct_links$d)
ct_mid <- c(mean(unlist(ct_links[far, c("x", "xend")])), mean(unlist(ct_links[far, c("y", "yend")])))
ct_top <- st_bbox(hunan)[["ymax"]] + 25000

ct_map <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = hunan, fill = "grey92", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_segment(data = ct_links, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
               colour = "grey45", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(data = ct_links, aes(x, y), size = 0.8) +
  geom_segment(data = ct_links[far, ], aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
               colour = "red", linewidth = 1,
               arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.15, "cm"))) +
  annotate("segment", x = ct_mid[1], y = ct_mid[2], xend = ct_mid[1], yend = ct_top,
           colour = "red", linewidth = 0.3) +
  annotate("label", x = ct_mid[1], y = ct_top, vjust = 0, size = 3.2, colour = "red",
           fill = "white", label.size = 0,
           label = paste0("critical_threshold(): the largest nearest-neighbour distance\n",
                          hunan$NAME_3[far], " to ", hunan$NAME_3[ct_nn[far]], ", ct = ",
                          format(round(ct, 2), big.mark = ","), " m")) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, ylim = c(st_bbox(hunan)["ymin"], ct_top + 90000)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_void()

ct_map
```
:::

`critical_threshold()` returns the smallest distance at which every county has at least one
neighbour, which is the rule on slide 36. Under EPSG:32649 the threshold is 62,955 m. Chapter 10
reports 60,800 m, the value of the same function under EPSG:32650. Section 5.1 examines the
difference.

```{r}
hunan_fdw <- hunan |>
  mutate(nb = include_self(st_dist_band(geometry, upper = ct)),
         wt = st_weights(nb, style = "W"),
         .before = 1)

summary(lengths(hunan_fdw$nb))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses three functions:

```r
st_dist_band(geometry, lower = 0,
             upper = critical_threshold(geometry))        # sfdep
include_self(nb)                                          # sfdep
lengths(x)                                                # base R
```

- `st_dist_band()` makes a county the neighbour of every county whose distance from it lies between
  `lower` and `upper`, here up to `ct` metres, since `hunan` is in EPSG:32649. For polygons, `sfdep`
  measures the distance between points on the surface of each county, from `st_point_on_surface()`,
  and `critical_threshold()` uses the same points.
- `upper` defaults to `critical_threshold(geometry)`, so passing `ct` gives the same band and shows
  the value used.
- `include_self()` adds each county to its own neighbour list, which turns Gi into Gi\*.
  `st_weights()` then row-standardises the weights as in section 4.1.1.
- `lengths()` returns the length of each element of a list, here the number of neighbours of each
  county, and `summary()` gives their minimum, quartiles, mean and maximum.

The figure applies the band to Taoyuan, the county that sets `ct`. The circle has radius `ct`
around Taoyuan's point, and a county is a neighbour when its point lies inside the circle.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 5
ty <- which(hunan$NAME_3 == "Taoyuan")
ty_nb <- hunan_fdw$nb[[ty]]
ty_circle <- st_buffer(ct_pts[ty], ct)
band_focus <- hunan |>
  mutate(role = case_when(row_number() == ty ~ "Taoyuan",
                          row_number() %in% ty_nb ~ "neighbour inside the band",
                          TRUE ~ "other"),
         role = factor(role, levels = c("Taoyuan", "neighbour inside the band", "other")))

ty_xy <- st_coordinates(ct_pts[ty])
band_top <- st_bbox(hunan)[["ymax"]] + 25000

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = band_focus, aes(fill = role), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_sf(data = ty_circle, fill = NA, colour = "red", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_sf(data = ct_pts, size = 0.8) +
  annotate("segment", x = ty_xy[1], y = ty_xy[2], xend = ty_xy[1], yend = band_top,
           colour = "red", linewidth = 0.3) +
  annotate("label", x = ty_xy[1], y = band_top, vjust = 0, size = 3.2, colour = "red",
           fill = "white",
           label = paste0("st_dist_band(upper = ct) + include_self()\n",
                          "circle of radius ct around Taoyuan\n",
                          "hunan_fdw$nb[[", ty, "]] = ", paste(ty_nb, collapse = ", "), ": ",
                          paste(hunan$NAME_3[ty_nb], collapse = " and "))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Taoyuan" = "darkorange",
                               "neighbour inside the band" = "#fdd49e", "other" = "grey92")) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, ylim = c(st_bbox(hunan)["ymin"], band_top + 110000)) +
  labs(fill = NULL) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Taoyuan's only neighbour is Hanshou, whose point lies exactly on the circle, and `include_self()`
adds Taoyuan itself. This is the sparsest neighbourhood in the province.
:::

`include_self()` distinguishes Gi\* from Gi. Gi excludes the county from its own neighbourhood, and
Gi\* includes it. Slide 27 gives both forms, and the chapter uses Gi\* throughout.

```{r}
hunan_adw <- hunan |>
  mutate(nb = include_self(st_knn(geometry, k = 6)),
         wt = st_weights(nb, style = "W"),
         .before = 1)

summary(lengths(hunan_adw$nb))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses one new function:

```r
st_knn(geometry, k = 1, symmetric = FALSE)                # sfdep
```

- `st_knn()` makes each county's `k` nearest counties its neighbours, measured between points on
  the surface of each county, as for `st_dist_band()` above. `k = 6` gives each county six.
- With `symmetric = FALSE`, the default, the list need not be symmetric: county A can be among
